newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FEATURE - PLO's Arafat resists checks on his power.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - PLO's Arafat resists checks on his power.

text.p: Yasser Arafat winces when lawmakers address Palestinian legislative council head Ahmed Korei as "president". It is a title many believe Arafat has trouble sharing.

Elected president of the Palestinian Authority 11 months ago by an overwhelming majority, Arafat appears unable to loosen the tight control he asserted as the PLO's guerrilla leader in exile for many years.

Palestinian legislators complain that Arafat refuses to yield to any form of checks on his authority. But the 88 legislators, chosen by the Palestinians of the West Bank and Gaza at the same time as Arafat, were elected to do just that.

"For the first time Abu Ammar faces a democratically elected council," said lawmaker Salah al-Taamari, using Arafat's nom de guerre. "He is not used to accountability and the word 'partnership' is not music to his ears."
It has been a learning process for both the executive and legislative branches.
The secretary-general of the Palestinian Authority, Ahmed Abdel-Rahman, defending the embryonic democracy, said: "The Authority is beginning to take steps towards accepting the accountability system.

"Ministers and officials have been summoned and questioned by the council, and the Authority has for the first time submitted its political, economic and social programme. This was never the case in the PLO," he told Reuters.
Lawmakers accuse Arafat, when in attendance at council sessions, of humiliating and marginalising them.
LOSES TEMPER OVER HUMAN RIGHTS CHARGES
Arafat lost his temper when facing criticism from legislators for alleged human rights abuses by his security forces.
When his arguments were challenged, Arafat would throw tantrums and storm out of sessions in anger, legislators said.
Council Speaker Korei, also known as Abu Ala, said that of the council's 134 decisions, only a few had actually been implemented by the Palestinian Authority.
Lawmakers said he had ignored their decisions, prompting 47 of them to threaten to call a no-confidence vote recently.
Legislator Kamal al-Shrafi said the move was not intended to bring the Authority down, but to remind it of the legislature's powers.
"The objective was to show the Authority there are legal measures that could be taken against its members if they continued ignoring the council's resolutions," Shrafi told Reuters.
"It is clear that Arafat tries to marginalise the council and does not respect its resolutions," said legislator Haidar Abdel-Shafi.
Legislators, mostly inexperienced in parliamentary traditions, have competed with Arafat and his authority for executive powers.
"There were many problems at the beginning. We the legislators also bypassed our limits and wanted to take up the role of the executive authority on some issues," Korei said.
ELECTIONS STEM FROM PEACE DEAL
The Palestinian elections last January were an integral part of the 1995 PLO-Israel interim peace deal.

For the first time in Palestinian history, Palestinians in the West Bank, including Arab East Jerusalem, and the Gaza Strip directly elected the president of the executive authority and 88 council members.
Five women and seven Islamists were among those elected. The majority of the council members belong to the PLO's mainstream Fatah faction and its supporters.
The council's powers are restricted by the peace deals since parts of the West Bank and Gaza Strip are still under Israeli occupation.
Almost half of the council members are from Gaza while the rest are from the West Bank, including East Jerusalem.

Lawmakers said their relationship with the Palestinian Authority and their effectiveness as legislators had been greatly harmed by Israeli restrictions, including a partial closure of the West Bank and Gaza.

"The most critical challenges we have faced since our election were Israeli deliberate obstacles to disrupt our work by hampering our movement from the West Bank to Gaza and vice versa where council sessions are held alternately," Korei said.
"Regardless of the difficulties, one of our most important achievements was the fact that the council has started to legislate," he said.
